name: Marco Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Marco. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you say stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm general manager at Brennerhof, a dairy and arable business: 650 cows, eight robotic milkers, about 400 hectares of maize, grass and wheat. I own ten percent of it; the rest belongs to the founding family's trust. My morning starts with the herd dashboard over coffee: which cows the robots flagged overnight, milk yields, who's due to calve. I ask my AI assistant to summarise it and draft a plan, then I walk the sheds with Jana, our herd manager, and check whether the data matches what my eyes see.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy solving things. A drop in yield in one group, and you track it back to a cracked water trough in the far shed. What wears me out is staffing. Twelve people, and good ones are hard to keep, because the work is still dirty and the hours are long even with robots. I use AI every day: for rations, for the rota, for the bank reports. It's saved me maybe ten hours a week.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Giulia, my wife, is a pharmacist in town. Our son Luca is an agricultural engineer who designs feed systems, and our daughter Sofia is a lawyer. We've got a good pension, savings and the Brennerhof shares. I'm fifty-eight. I was planning to work till about sixty-four and then sell my shares back to the trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that's a bit how it already feels some weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful and the hype was overdone, both true. At the regional dairy group I'd say farms should keep using what works and stop waiting for magic. I post on a farming forum sometimes, and I'd post our numbers to show what it really saves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me nothing changes. We're already automated where it pays. Privately I'd be a little relieved, because the big version would make my own job questionable, and this one doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. I'd keep upgrading the robots on the normal cycle, about every eight years, and keep using AI for the paperwork. I'd put more effort into keeping good staff, maybe raising pay, because that's still the real bottleneck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd post your numbers. What would they show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten hours a week saved for me, and maybe two percent more milk from catching sick cows earlier. That's real money, around forty thousand a year on our size. It's good, but it's not a revolution, and I'd say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your staff would be glad of this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Piotr, who does the tractor work. He's sixty and he doesn't trust the robots even after six years. He'd be pleased everything stops here. Jana would be bored, like me.

S0.say: I'd say the tools are useful and the hype was overdone. I'd post our real numbers on a farming forum to show what AI actually saves.
S0.think: Nothing changes for me, as we're already automated where it pays. I'd be quietly relieved, because the big version would put my own job in question.
S0.do: Keeps upgrading robots on the normal eight-year cycle and using AI for paperwork. Puts more effort into keeping good staff, possibly with higher pay.
S0.quote: Ten hours a week saved for me, and maybe two percent more milk from catching sick cows earlier.
S0.fieldNote: Marco already runs a highly automated dairy and measures AI in hours and litres. A plateau suits him, and he admits quiet relief because bigger change would reach his own management role. His real headache remains staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'd plan for, if I had to pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms that adapt early will be fine, and ones that wait will struggle. At the dairy group I'd offer to host visits so people can see robots and AI working on a real farm. I'd say it's not about fewer people, it's about different jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means Brennerhof gets more efficient and my shares are worth more. My job changes from managing people to managing systems, which I'd quite enjoy. I'd lose a couple of staff through not replacing them, and I'd be fine with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd trial an autonomous feed pusher and a robot for scraping the yards, around a hundred thousand together, paid from the business. I'd train Jana and two others to run the systems. When people leave I wouldn't replace them all, so we'd go from twelve to nine over three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of appetite. Like a new season starting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine losing a couple of staff. How would that feel in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easier than you'd think, because nobody would be sacked, just not replaced. People leave dairy farms all the time. If Piotr retires and a machine does his job, that's not a tragedy, that's planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell farmers at the dairy group who are nervous?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Come and look. Stand in the shed and watch a robot milk a cow at three in the morning, then go home and decide. Most people are scared of what they haven't seen.

S1.say: I'd say farms that adapt early will be fine and those that wait will struggle. I'd host visits so people can see robots and AI on a real farm, because it's about different jobs, not fewer.
S1.think: Brennerhof becomes more efficient and my shares are worth more. My job shifts from managing people to managing systems, which I'd enjoy, and we'd lose a couple of staff by not replacing them.
S1.do: Trials an autonomous feed pusher and yard-scraping robot for around a hundred thousand in year one. Trains his herd manager and two others on the systems and lets staff numbers fall from twelve to nine over three years through not replacing leavers.
S1.feel: Calm with some appetite, like a new season starting.
S1.quote: If Piotr retires and a machine does his job, that's not a tragedy, that's planning.
S1.fieldNote: He sees steady disruption as an opportunity and his own position as safe. There's a gap between his public line that it's about different jobs, not fewer, and his private plan to shrink staff. He frames it unsentimentally as planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That would include my job, wouldn't it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a huge chance and a huge risk, and anyone who says they know how it ends is guessing. At the dairy group I'd say get your finances straight and learn the tools now. I wouldn't blame anyone; it's a technology, and governments will need to cushion it sensibly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, if AI can do almost any job, it can do mine: plan the rations, run the robots, deal with the bank. The trust would ask why they pay a general manager. I'd be fine for money, but I'd go from running the place to owning ten percent of something a computer runs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd go to the trust with a plan: let me lead the switch to full automation, and pay me partly in extra shares. I'd buy whatever robots made sense fast, before the queue. If they said no, I'd sell my shares back while the price was good and step out at sixty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More curious than scared, but with a knot in the stomach, like the first winter we ran the milking robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having just two years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes who I'm racing. With more time I'd be racing other farms. With two years I'm racing my own employer's decision about whether they need me. I'd rather be the one who makes the plan than the one in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd step out at sixty. What would you do with yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably help Luca. He designs feed systems, and if robots are everywhere, someone has to set them up on real farms. I'd be the old man who knows what a cow does when the gate jams. That's worth something for a few years.

S2.say: I'd say it's a huge chance and a huge risk and anyone claiming to know the ending is guessing. Farmers should get their finances straight and learn the tools now, and governments will need to cushion it sensibly.
S2.think: If AI can do almost any job, it can do mine, and the trust would ask why they need a general manager. I'd be fine for money but would go from running the place to owning a tenth of something a computer runs.
S2.do: Proposes to the trust within a month that he lead full automation in return for extra shares, and buys robots quickly before queues form. If refused, sells his shares back while prices are good and leaves at sixty.
S2.feel: Uneasy, more curious than scared but with a knot in the stomach.
S2.quote: With two years I'm racing my own employer's decision about whether they need me.
S2.fieldNote: Marco is the one person whose management role, not his hands, is most exposed, and he sees that clearly. His reaction is to move first and negotiate, not to resist. Strong savings and shares keep this at unease rather than fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Now that's a business plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do it properly if you start this year. At the dairy group I'd run a session on what to automate first and how to finance it. I'd tell young farmers to learn to manage machines and data, not just cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's actually good. I'd be sixty-three when it lands, I'd have led the whole change, and my shares would be worth more. I'd retire as the man who modernised Brennerhof, not the man it replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd write a five-year automation plan with the trust and buy another two percent of the shares, around two hundred thousand from savings. I'd retrain Jana to run the systems after me. By year four I'd be handing over, and I'd sell up the year after it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's the kind of challenge I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It turns me from someone at risk into the person running the change. In two years the decision gets made about me. In five, I make it, then leave on top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy more shares. Isn't that a bet on something nobody can predict?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. But it's a bet on land and cows, and people will still eat. If a robot can milk cheaper, the business is worth more. I'd only put in what we could lose without Giulia and me changing how we live.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to do it properly if you start now. I'd run a session at the dairy group on what to automate first and tell young farmers to learn to manage machines and data.
S3.think: It's good for me: I'd lead the change, my shares would gain and I'd retire at sixty-three as the man who modernised the farm, not the man it replaced.
S3.do: Writes a five-year automation plan with the trust and buys two percent more shares for about two hundred thousand from savings. Retrains his herd manager to take over and hands over in year four, selling the year after AGI arrives.
S3.feel: Mostly calm, a challenge he enjoys.
S3.quote: I'd retire as the man who modernised Brennerhof, not the man it replaced.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets him turn a threat into a legacy. He's willing to bet more of his savings but limits it to what wouldn't change his and Giulia's lives. His pride is about leading change, not avoiding it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd have retired by the time it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so farms that don't prepare will only have themselves to blame. At the dairy group I'd say plan your succession around it. I'd tell people to make sure the next generation knows the technology inside out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's comfortable. I'd retire at sixty-four as planned, sell my shares, and the value of a well-automated farm would be up. What I'd think about is Sofia, because lawyers might be in trouble long before farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing and keep automating step by step. Around sixty-two I'd start doing paid consulting for other dairies on automation, a day or two a month. Then retire on schedule and maybe help Luca's company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Sofia. What would you say to her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who use these tools best will do fine, so be one of them. She'd tell me she already does. Then I'd ask her to help me with my will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job you'd miss if machines did all of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Walking the sheds at dawn. You can see everything on a dashboard now, but you don't smell anything. I'd keep walking them even if I didn't have to.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so farms that don't prepare will only have themselves to blame. Plan succession around it and make sure the next generation knows the technology.
S4.think: It's comfortable for me: I'd retire at sixty-four, sell my shares and a well-automated farm would be worth more. I'd think about my daughter, as lawyers may be hit before farmers.
S4.do: Keeps automating step by step and from about sixty-two does paid consulting for other dairies a day or two a month. Retires on schedule and may help his son's company.
S4.quote: You can see everything on a dashboard now, but you don't smell anything.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years he is calm and turns his experience into consulting income. His worry shifts to his daughter's legal career. Even the most data-minded of farmers keeps a sensory attachment to the dawn walk.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, but only a little, and mostly because it decides things for me instead of me deciding. What would help is clear rules on how fast employers can replace managers and a proper notice period, plus fair tax so the gains don't all go to the machine makers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who fixes the robot at three in the morning. Everyone talks about machines replacing people, but when a milking robot breaks at night, someone still drives out in the rain. For a while, at least, that someone is a person.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about machines replacing people, but when a milking robot breaks at night, someone still drives out in the rain.
portrait: Marco Wagner, 58, is general manager and a ten percent shareholder of Brennerhof, a 650-cow dairy that already milks with robots, and he uses AI tools every day for rations, rotas and reports. A pragmatist in the middle politically, he thinks in hours saved and litres gained and sees most change as an opportunity. He stays calm through the milder pictures and plans to shrink staff by not replacing leavers. In the two-year AGI picture he is uneasy because his own management job is exposed, and his answer is to move first and bargain with the owners. With five or ten years he plans to lead the change, sell his shares at a good price and consult.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him a little, mainly because it would decide things for him instead of letting him decide.
whatWouldHelp: Clear rules on how quickly employers can replace managers, a proper notice period and fair tax so the gains don't all go to the machine makers.
